title: Functionalism: Society as a System
description: Parsons's grand theory, the sick role, and why functionalism fell from favour

concepts.title: Parsons and the Problem of Order
concepts.contentHtml:
Every society poses a puzzle. Millions of people pursue their own ends, yet most days the buses run, shops open and strangers keep their promises. A social theory tries to explain patterns like this: why social life holds together, why it changes, and how individual choices add up to institutions. This topic follows the main answers given since the 1930s. The founders they build on, Marx, Durkheim and Weber, have their own topic, Classical Social Theory.

The answer that dominated mid-century sociology came from Talcott Parsons (1902–1979), who taught at Harvard from 1927 to 1974. His first book, The Structure of Social Action (1937), argued that the classical theorists were converging on a voluntaristic theory of action: people choose between means and ends, but inside a physical and social environment that limits their choices. At the London School of Economics he had studied with the anthropologist Bronisław Malinowski and taken from him a view of society as a system of interrelated parts.1 In The Social System (1951) Parsons pictured society that way: parts held together by shared norms and values, tending towards equilibrium.

His best-known device is the AGIL scheme. Any lasting system, Parsons said, must solve four problems, and in a society each is handled mainly by one subsystem:2

  • Adaptation: getting resources from the environment (the economy).
  • Goal attainment: setting and pursuing collective goals (the political system).
  • Integration: coordinating the parts and handling differences (the societal community and institutions of social control, such as law).
  • Latency, or pattern maintenance: passing on and renewing values (socialisation through family, school and religion).

Explaining an institution by what it contributes to the whole is structural functionalism. Parsons wrapped it in a vast vocabulary of pattern variables and two-by-two tables, and his students carried it into departments around the world in the 1950s and 1960s.

concepts.title: The Sick Role: Functionalism at Work
concepts.contentHtml:
Parsons's most durable idea is small and concrete. Disease, he argued in The Social System (1951), is a bodily matter, but being sick, being recognised and accepted as ill, is a social role governed by expectations,1 just like being a teacher or a parent. He listed four:

  • The sick person is exempt from normal duties, but only once an authority, usually a doctor, legitimates the claim.
  • They are not held responsible for being ill, so others must look after them.
  • Because sickness is undesirable, they are obliged to want to get better.
  • They must seek technically competent help and cooperate with it.

Here is functionalism at work. If anyone could stop working whenever they felt unwell, a society would struggle to get its work done. Parsons, who had trained in psychoanalysis, thought illness often had motives of its own, so he treated it as a special form of deviance and medicine as a mechanism of social control: it restores the sick to health and makes sure only the genuinely ill are excused. The doctor's sick note is the whole theory in miniature, a gatekeeper certifying that your absence is legitimate.

The concept became central to medical sociology; one standard dictionary says its importance would be hard to overestimate. It also exposes functionalism's weak spots. Critics have questioned whether the four expectations hold in every culture, how far illness is really motivated, and what the model says about2 chronic illness, where getting better is not on offer and the duty to recover makes little sense. They also objected to its focus on what is functional for society rather than for the patient. Parsons himself was diabetic for the last twenty years of his life.

concepts.title: Why Functionalism Fell, and What Survived
concepts.contentHtml:
By the late 1960s functionalism was under fire. C. Wright Mills mocked Parsons in The Sociological Imagination (1959) and gave the approach a label that stuck, grand theory: abstract theorising in which arranging concepts takes priority over understanding the social world. Alvin Gouldner's The Coming Crisis of Western Sociology (1970) finished the job. As the post-war consensus cracked under the impact of the Vietnam War, a theory of equilibrium and shared values looked like a theory of the status quo. It could not, critics said, explain change, conflict or power, and its organic analogy made it conservative.

Those political charges are only partly accurate. Parsons did have a theory of change: societies evolve by differentiating into more specialised subsystems and then reintegrating them. The criticisms that really bite are logical:

  • No mechanism. Explaining an institution by its effects does not show how those effects brought it into being.1
  • Societies do not have needs. Even if a society needs integration, nothing guarantees that the need will be met; showing how it is met takes a historical, causal account. Anthony Giddens argued that every functionalist explanation can be rewritten as a story of human actions and their consequences.

Yet functional reasoning never died. Herbert Gans's 1972 essay ‘The Positive Functions of Poverty’ asked what poverty does for everyone else; some read it as a parody of functionalism, while one standard dictionary calls it a superb example of ideologically neutral functional analysis. Jeffrey Alexander revived a looser neofunctionalism in the 1980s, and Niklas Luhmann built systems theory in Germany. Even Jon Elster, a leading rational-choice theorist, accepts one kind of functional explanation:2 whatever their origins, firms that come closest to maximising profit are the ones the market selects for survival. Functional explanation works best where you can name the selection mechanism. Sibling topics apply the approach: Social Stratification examines Davis and Moore's functional theory of inequality, and Deviance teaches Merton's strain theory.

title: Merton: Functions, Prophecies and the Middle Range
description: Latent functions, self-fulfilling prophecies, what Pygmalion really found, and middle-range theory

concepts.title: Manifest and Latent Functions
concepts.contentHtml:
Robert K. Merton made functionalism testable. He was born Meyer R. Schkolnick on 4 July 1910 to working-class Jewish immigrants in South Philadelphia, took his doctorate at Harvard in 1936 and trained generations of students at Columbia. In Social Theory and Social Structure (1949) he insisted on separating what people intend from what their actions actually do.

Manifest functions are consequences that are intended and recognised; latent functions are unintended and unrecognised. Merton adapted the terms from Freud. His classic case is the Hopi rain ceremonial. Meteorologists agree that the ceremony does not produce rain, he wrote, but this is hardly to the point.1 Labelling it superstition ends the inquiry. Asking about latent functions continues it, by examining what the ceremony does for the group that performs it: it provides a periodic occasion for scattered members to assemble in a common activity, and so reinforces group identity. Apparently irrational behaviour may turn out to be functional.

His second case came from industry. At the Western Electric company's Hawthorne plant in the 1920s, engineers varied the lighting to see how output changed. Merton reports that output rose both in the experimental group, whose lighting was changed, and in the control group, whose lighting was not, and that it took years for the researchers to turn to the latent social functions of the informal groups forming among workers. Wait, really? In 2009 the economists Steven Levitt and John List found the original illumination data, long thought destroyed, and concluded that the famous descriptions of remarkable data patterns were entirely fictional, though they saw hints of subtler effects.2

Merton also coined dysfunction for consequences that weaken a system, and among leading functionalists he was particularly attentive to dysfunction, historical change and conflict. His 1938 paper on anomie, the root of strain theory, is taught in the Deviance topic.

concepts.title: Self-Fulfilling Prophecies and Pygmalion
concepts.contentHtml:
Merton gave a name to one of social science's most famous mechanisms. W. I. Thomas had observed that when people define situations as real, they become real in their consequences. Merton's self-fulfilling prophecy is the special case where the definition starts out false: a false belief evokes new behaviour that makes the originally false conception come true. (The Hyperstition topic follows the idea through bank runs and markets.) The word ‘false’ matters: a prediction that comes true because it was accurate is not self-fulfilling.

The best-known test came from a school. In Pygmalion in the Classroom (1968), Rosenthal and Jacobson gave every child in Jacobson's elementary school, from kindergarten to fifth grade, a nonverbal IQ test disguised as a new Harvard test for spotting children about to ‘bloom’. They then told each teacher which pupils were likely late bloomers. These children, about 20 per cent of the school, had in fact been chosen at random. A year later the ‘bloomers’ had gained about 12 IQ points and the other children about 8.

The popular version stops there: tell teachers a child is bright and the child becomes brighter. Lee Jussim and Kent Harber's 2005 review gives the fuller picture:

  • The average difference between bloomers and controls was about 4 IQ points, and it came almost entirely from the first and second grades.
  • Raudenbush's 1984 meta-analysis of 18 experiments found a very small effect on IQ (d = 0.11). Expectations planted in the first two weeks of the school year had an effect; those planted later had none.
  • Across 35 years of research, classroom self-fulfilling prophecies do occur, but they are typically small and more likely to fade than to accumulate.1 They may be stronger among students from stigmatised groups.
  • Teachers' expectations predict how pupils do mainly because they are accurate.

concepts.title: Theories of the Middle Range
concepts.contentHtml:
Merton's deepest disagreement with Parsons was about method. Grand theory tried to explain everything at once; narrow empirical studies piled up findings without theory. Merton argued for theories of the middle range, which he placed between the minor working hypotheses of day-to-day research and all-inclusive attempts at a unified theory of society. A middle-range theory names a specific mechanism, can be tested, and can sit inside several larger frameworks at once.

His own career is the best advertisement. Many of his coinages are now ordinary vocabulary: role model, self-fulfilling prophecy, reference group and the unanticipated consequences of purposive social action (the title of a 1936 paper). He showed that people often judge their opportunities not in objective terms but by comparison with a chosen reference group, which is why relative deprivation can make the better-off feel worse off. With Marjorie Fiske and Patricia Kendall he invented the focused group interview (1956), ancestor of the now ubiquitous, and not always systematic, focus groups of political and market research.

The most quoted example is the Matthew effect, presented to the American Sociological Association in 1967 and published in Science the following year. Credit in science tends to accrue to scientists who are already well known.1 Merton named it after the Gospel of Matthew (25:29): ‘For unto every one that hath shall be given, and he shall have abundance.’ The idea of cumulative advantage it launched now runs through research on citations, careers and wealth.

Middle-range theory became the working method of much empirical sociology, and in 1994 Merton became the first sociologist to receive the US National Medal of Science. Its limitation is that a collection of well-tested mechanisms is not yet a picture of how a whole society fits together; the syntheses of Giddens and Bourdieu later in this topic try to supply one.

title: Power and Critique: From Conflict Theory to Habermas
description: Conflict theory and the power elite, The Authoritarian Personality, and the public sphere

concepts.title: Conflict Theory and the Power Elite
concepts.contentHtml:
Functionalism asked how societies hold together. Conflict theory asks who gains, who loses and who gives the orders. Its roots are in Marx and Weber, taught in Classical Social Theory, but in the 1950s a group of sociologists turned it against the Parsonian consensus:

  • Ralf Dahrendorf (Class and Class Conflict in Industrial Society, 1959) based conflict on power rather than property. In any organisation, order-givers have an interest in keeping the status quo and order-takers an interest in changing it.
  • Lewis Coser (The Functions of Social Conflict, 1956), developing Georg Simmel, showed that conflict has effects of its own: it centralises power within each side and drives groups to seek allies. Conflict, in other words, can itself be functional.
  • Randall Collins (Conflict Sociology, 1975) traced the differences between stratified groups to the micro-interactions of daily experience, along two dimensions: vertical power and horizontal solidarity.

The loudest voice was C. Wright Mills, born in Waco, Texas, in 1916, who saw himself as a rebel against the social-science establishment. He was no enemy of data, but he attacked ‘abstracted empiricism’ as fiercely as grand theory and held up the ideal of the sociologist as a craftsman. In The Power Elite (1956) he argued that the United States was run by an élite of business, government and military leaders, bound together by shared social backgrounds and by people moving between the three.1

The book provoked a long controversy. Critics such as Daniel Bell and the political scientist Robert Dahl rejected the picture of a single, unified élite, and the argument between élite theorists and their critics shaped decades of research on who holds power. Mills became an acid critic of the so-called military-industrial complex and one of the earliest leaders of the New Left. Conflict theory's legacy is the habit of asking, of any institution, whose interests it serves.

concepts.title: The Frankfurt School Goes Empirical
concepts.contentHtml:
The Frankfurt School takes its name from the Institute for Social Research, founded in Frankfurt in 1923. When Max Horkheimer became its director in 1931, he proposed a programme combining philosophy and social theory with psychology, political economy and cultural analysis. Its most famous ideas, the culture industry and one-dimensional society, are taught in the Media Theory and Marxism topics. This concept looks at its largest piece of empirical sociology.

The Authoritarian Personality (1950) came from research by Theodor Adorno, who had fled the Third Reich, with a team of psychologists at the University of California, Berkeley: Else Frenkel-Brunswik, Daniel Levinson and Nevitt Sanford. They asked why some people are more susceptible to fascism than others, and looked not at party membership but at personality and social attitudes, measured with attitude scales. The most famous was the F-scale, F for fascism. Across more than 2,000 respondents, a set of traits clustered together:1 ethnocentrism, rigid adherence to conventional values, submission to the moral authority of the in-group, a readiness to punish, and an unwillingness to tolerate ambiguity. Intensive interviews then linked the pattern, through Freudian theory, to families marked by rigid discipline and fearful obedience to parents. A companion study, Prophets of Deceit, analysed the messages of the agitators themselves.

The book had a major impact on political sociology, inspiring a wave of similar studies, and its title entered everyday language. It also drew heavy criticism:

  • It measured only an authoritarianism of the right and ignored the closed mind of the left.
  • Like all theories of scapegoating, it tended to reduce complex historical processes to psychological needs.
  • Its scales and samples were flawed.

The lasting lesson is methodological as much as political. The Frankfurt theorists, often remembered as pure philosophers, also ran surveys, and although their methods have not aged well, their question, which ordinary people are receptive to authoritarian messages and why, remains a live one.

concepts.title: Habermas and the Public Sphere
concepts.contentHtml:
Jürgen Habermas, the leading figure of the Frankfurt School's second generation, made his name with The Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere (1962), his habilitation thesis. The public sphere belongs to neither the state, the economy nor the family: it is where private individuals come together to communicate about matters of general concern.

Habermas reconstructed its rise and fall in Britain, France and Germany. In the Middle Ages there was only a ‘representative’ public sphere, in which kings and nobles displayed their status before society. In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries a new reading public met in coffee houses, salons and literary societies, at first to discuss novels such as Samuel Richardson's Pamela, then to criticise government. Differences of status were bracketed as private matters, so in principle only the argument counted. Then came decline. In twentieth-century welfare-state mass democracy, parties, corporations and pressure groups negotiated with the state over the public's head, and public relations replaced public reason. Habermas called this refeudalisation: as in the feudal era, the public's role became to acclaim decisions already made.

Critics pressed on the history. The actual participants were almost all educated, male, property-owning members of the bourgeoisie. Historians argued that the public sphere was built by excluding propertyless workers and, above all, women, as Joan Landes argued for revolutionary France.1 Nancy Fraser showed that excluded groups formed subaltern counterpublics of their own. Habermas now concedes that a society contains many intersecting public spheres with porous boundaries.2

The concept survives because it works as a yardstick: Habermas called the bourgeois public sphere both an ideal and an ideology. You can measure any forum, from a parliament to a comment section, against open, status-blind argument while knowing that none has fully met it. His later theory of communicative action and the colonisation of the lifeworld is covered in the Marxism topic.

title: Selves in Interaction: Mead, Blumer and Goffman
description: How selves form in interaction, Goffman's stagecraft, and life inside total institutions

concepts.title: Mead and Blumer: The Social Self
concepts.contentHtml:
While Parsons studied systems, a rival tradition studied encounters. It began with George Herbert Mead (1863–1931), who chaired the philosophy department at the University of Chicago. His most famous work, Mind, Self, and Society (1934), was published after his death and is a compilation of student notes and unpublished manuscripts.

Mead's claim was that the self is not given at birth but built by taking the attitudes of others. A small child plays at being a doctor by anticipating what a patient would say. A game demands more: to play second base in baseball you must think of yourself in relation to the whole game, the other players and the rules. That organised community, taken inside, is the generalised other. Mead also split the self into two phases. The ‘me’ is the self as it arises in relation to others, known only on reflection. The ‘I’ is the spontaneous, creative response, which you can only catch afterwards, by which time it has already become a ‘me’.

The sociologist Herbert Blumer coined the term symbolic interactionism in 1937 and in 1969 set out three premises:

  • Human beings act towards things on the basis of the meanings the things have for them.
  • Those meanings arise out of social interaction.
  • Meanings are handled in, and modified through, an interpretive process.

Interactionists worked by close observation of doctors, dance-band musicians, drug users and the dying, and they shaped the labelling theory of deviance. During functionalism's heyday they were called ‘the loyal opposition’. Their weakness mirrored Parsons's: in the 1970s interactionism attracted considerable criticism for its neglect of social structure, power and history.1 Sheldon Stryker answered by tying interaction back to roles and the social structures that allow people more or less room to make their roles rather than simply take them.

concepts.title: Goffman: Social Life as Theatre
concepts.contentHtml:
Erving Goffman, born in Alberta, Canada, in 1922, was the most influential micro-sociologist of the 1960s and 1970s. His method began on a small island. Based in Edinburgh, he spent from December 1949 to May 1951 on Unst, in Shetland, studying a crofting community for his doctoral thesis, and those observations fed The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life (1959).

The book treats social life as theatre. In front regions, official definitions of reality are presented to an audience; in back regions, dirty work is hidden and performances are prepared. Think of a waiter who is all deference in the dining room and mocks the customers in the kitchen, or a doctor who reassures a patient and then confers anxiously with colleagues. Everyone engages in impression management, controlling the picture of themselves that others receive. Goffman added a political edge that is easy to miss: privileged occupations and social classes dominate frontstages and present idealised images of themselves and their institutions, while subordinated people do much of their work backstage.1

His later essays applied Durkheim's ideas about ritual to greetings, departures and conversation (‘On Face-Work’, 1955), and Frame Analysis (1974) studied how people decide what kind of situation they are in, an idea media scholars borrowed for news framing (see Bias and Framing). He also studied confidence games, spying and embarrassment, because odd situations reveal the conditions that hold ordinary reality in place.

Not everyone admired the picture. Alvin Gouldner's The Coming Crisis of Western Sociology cast Goffman as an apologist for capitalism, overly cynical and far too concerned with the trivial. The defence is that the trivial is where social order is actually produced, and that a theory of performance is not an endorsement of the play.

concepts.title: Total Institutions: Asylums and Its Critics
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1955 Goffman moved to Washington, DC, and began a year of fieldwork at St Elizabeths Hospital, a federal psychiatric hospital that held more than 7,000 patients by the mid-1950s.1 The result, Asylums (1961), introduced the total institution: a place where people sleep, work and play inside the same walls, are processed in blocks by a bureaucracy, and are cut off from the normal round of life. Prisons and mental hospitals were his key examples, but he included barracks, boarding schools, monasteries and concentration camps.

Goffman traced the moral career of a mental patient. Admission brings mortification: newcomers are dispossessed of their civilian selves and pressed into a new self-understanding as mental patients. Inmates resist through an underlife of small adjustments that preserve a sense of self beyond the institution's control, behaviour that can look bizarre to staff. His sharpest claim was that such regimentation, rather than promoting recovery, produced the very disordered behaviour for which people had supposedly been admitted.

Asylums became a key text of the anti-psychiatry movement of the 1960s and of a wider critique of social control. But a closer look at St Elizabeths complicates it. The physician and historian Matthew Gambino, drawing on writings by patients and staff, found a richer and more dynamic patient culture than Asylums suggests: patient-run journals, art and dance therapy, psychodrama, and an elected Patients' Administrative Group. Within a year of Goffman's departure, patients formed a Patients' Federation representing every ward.2 Goffman had found little evidence of meaningful bonds among patients. Gambino concedes that the innovations reached wards for acutely ill patients far more than those for long-stay patients. The model was built to show how institutions crush selves; it is weaker at seeing how people organise inside them. (Goffman's next book, Stigma, is taught in the Deviance topic.)

title: Making Order: Garfinkel, Coleman and Giddens
description: Breaching experiments, the timing of talk, rational choice, and structuration and its critics

concepts.title: Garfinkel and the Breaching Experiments
concepts.contentHtml:
Harold Garfinkel studied under Parsons at Harvard and then, through some twenty years of research at UCLA, turned his teacher's question inside out. Parsons asked how shared norms produce order. Garfinkel asked how ordinary people produce, moment by moment, the sense that there is an order at all. He called the study of their everyday methods ethnomethodology, and he insisted that people are not ‘cultural dopes’ following rules but sophisticated practical reasoners.

His best-known technique is the breaching experiment: break an unspoken rule and watch people scramble to repair it. In Studies in Ethnomethodology (1967) he describes asking students to spend 15 to 60 minutes at home acting as polite boarders: formal address, nothing personal, speaking only when spoken to. Nine of the 49 could not carry it out.1 Elsewhere families reacted with astonishment, bewilderment, shock, embarrassment or anger and demanded explanations: ‘What's the matter?’ ‘Are you sick?’ One student's sister replied for her family: ‘Please, no more of these experiments. We're not rats, you know.’ In another exercise, students kept asking ‘What do you mean?’ about ordinary remarks until their partners became distressed and angry.

Conversation analysis, associated with Harvey Sacks, took the same attitude to recorded talk and found rules such as ‘one speaker at a time’. Anthropologists had claimed that some cultures prize long silences and others constant overlap. A 2009 study led by Tanya Stivers compared video of natural conversation in 10 languages from five continents. Every language showed a general avoidance of overlap and a minimisation of silence between turns. Japanese replies came fastest on average (+7 milliseconds) and Danish slowest (+469),2 but in every language the most common gap was between 0 and 200 milliseconds.

Critics such as John Goldthorpe and James Coleman found ethnomethodology trivial, and breaching raises obvious ethical problems. Yet its core insight, that order is continually accomplished in talk and action, is now almost taken for granted.

concepts.title: Rational Choice: Coleman and the Micro–Macro Problem
concepts.contentHtml:
Rational-choice theory gives a different answer to the problem of order: order is the unplanned outcome of individuals pursuing their own advantage. Its roots run back to Adam Smith, and George Homans and Peter Blau built exchange theories on it. Its most ambitious sociological statement is Foundations of Social Theory (1990) by James S. Coleman (1926–1995), also a major figure in the sociology of education. His Equality of Educational Opportunity (1966), the Coleman Report, was a national study of 600,000 students, 60,000 teachers and 4,000 public schools1 that demonstrated the importance of non-school factors, such as family background, for children's achievement.

Coleman's key tool is a diagram often called Coleman's boat. Its top line joins two facts about whole societies, for example Weber's famous thesis linking Calvinism to capitalism. Coleman held that the sociologist's goal is always to explain the macro outcome, but that the direct arrow between the two explains nothing until it is broken into steps through individuals: how the macro situation shapes people's circumstances and beliefs, how they then act, and how their actions combine into a new macro outcome. The last step is the hardest.

Its classic illustration is Mancur Olson's logic of collective action (1965). If a group's shared goal requires each member to pay a personal cost, a narrowly self-interested member will hope to free ride on others' contributions, so shared interests alone do not produce collective action. That explains why many groups never organise, and turns every social movement, and every election in which millions bother to vote, into a puzzle the theory must solve.

Critics make three objections. Sociology has no common currency, like money, for measuring advantage. Because any action can be redescribed as maximising something, the theory veers towards tautology. And, following Durkheim, stable exchange depends on pre-existing trust and law, so it cannot be their source. Coleman's own response was social capital, taken up in the Social Networks topic.

concepts.title: Giddens: Structuration and Its Critics
concepts.contentHtml:
If Garfinkel started from situated action and Coleman from individual choice, Anthony Giddens tried to dissolve the split between action and structure altogether. His structuration theory, set out in Central Problems in Social Theory (1979) and The Constitution of Society (1984), rejects functionalism and evolutionary theory as closed systems and puts social practices at the centre. Structures, for Giddens, are not something external to people but rules and resources that actors draw on and reproduce in their practices.

His key phrase is the duality of structure: structure is both the medium and outcome of the reproduction of practices. Think of a language. You cannot say anything without its grammar, yet the grammar exists only because millions of people keep speaking, and it drifts as they do. Giddens drew openly on ethnomethodology here, treating the taken-for-granted rules of talk and action as the hinge between the two. He also stressed time and space, and went on to write a historical sociology of the nation-state and modernity.

The critics were blunt. Some accused Giddens of reinventing the wheel, and of obscurantism and empirical emptiness, a charge that drew an unflattering parallel with Parsons. The most influential alternative came from the critical realist Margaret Archer. Her analytic dualism is the claim that effective research depends on a clear distinction between actors and structures.1 Structures depend on activity, she argues, but they are the effects of past actions, often by long-dead people, which survive them; you meet them as conditions you did not choose, so you need to study how they shape you separately from how you change them. Nicos Mouzelis added that a single worker relates to a huge organisation as an outside object she cannot influence, not as a duality she reproduces. Bourdieu, in the next lesson, offered a third route through the same problem.

title: Bourdieu: Habitus, Field and Capital
description: Habitus and field, the forms of capital, and what surveys of taste have found since Distinction

concepts.title: Habitus and Field
concepts.contentHtml:
Pierre Bourdieu (1930–2002) was born in Denguin, in south-western France, and went from the lycée in nearby Pau to the Lycée Louis-le-Grand and the École normale supérieure in Paris. His first research was in Algeria, where he taught at the faculty of letters in Algiers from 1958 to 1960. His central question was how social structures get inside people and come back out as practice.

His answer is habitus: a set of acquired patterns of thought, behaviour and taste that links social structures to social practice.1 A childhood in a particular social position shows up decades later as an accent, a posture, a sense of what is or is not ‘for people like us’, and an instinct for what to do next that works without calculation. Habitus operates within fields: relatively autonomous arenas such as art, science, law or the academic world, each with its own stakes and its own valued resources. The structure of a field is the unequal distribution of capital within it, and those who hold the most can impose the rules that suit them best.

When habitus and field match, action feels natural. ‘Innocence,’ Bourdieu wrote, ‘is the privilege of those who move in their field of activity like fish in water.’ When they do not, as for a first-generation student at an elite university, the same situation can feel like a test of rules nobody ever explained.

Habitus is meant to escape the choice between seeing people as puppets of structure and seeing them as free calculators. Bourdieu insisted that the objective and subjective sides of social life are inescapably bound together, and so challenged the dualisms of macro and micro, structure and agency. Whether he succeeded is disputed. Some critics find habitus notoriously elusive, and one standard dictionary doubts that his diverse books form a systematic project at all, far less solve the problem of structure and agency.

concepts.title: The Forms of Capital
concepts.contentHtml:
In ‘The Forms of Capital’ (1986), Bourdieu argued that economics sees only one kind of capital, money and whatever converts directly into it, and so misses most of how advantage is passed on. He distinguished:

  • Economic capital: money and property.
  • Cultural capital, in three states: embodied (knowledge, manners and taste, built up through years of personal investment), objectified (books, instruments, paintings) and institutionalised (qualifications).
  • Social capital: resources that come from membership of a durable network of mutual acquaintance and recognition.
  • Symbolic capital: any capital when it is perceived as legitimate prestige or competence rather than as capital.

Embodied cultural capital is the subtle one. Like the acquisition of a muscular physique or a suntan, Bourdieu wrote, it cannot be done at second hand.1 It takes time, and time is what money buys: the free time in which a family can pass on culture and delay children's entry into work. Human-capital economists such as Gary Becker, he complained, treated academic ability as natural and forgot that ability or talent is itself the product of an investment of time and cultural capital.2 Because cultural transmission inside the family is diffuse and escapes observation, schools seem to reward natural gifts while in fact rewarding inherited advantage. This disguised conversion of privilege into apparent merit is the root of what Bourdieu called symbolic violence.

The degree is the clever part. A qualification gives its holder a conventional, legally guaranteed value independent of what they actually know on a given day, and it lets employers compare holders. But its value depends on scarcity, so as qualifications spread, the conversion rate between academic and economic capital can fall: the same degree buys less than it did. Social Stratification follows these mechanisms into schools and mobility data; Coleman's rival idea of social capital appears in Social Networks.

concepts.title: Distinction and Its Tests
concepts.contentHtml:
Bourdieu's most famous book, Distinction (1979, English translation 1984), mapped the tastes of French adults in the 1960s in music, food, art, sport and home décor. Using correspondence analysis, a technique that turns a large table of survey answers into a map showing which answers cluster together, he found taste lining up with class position. Preferences, he argued, are not innocent: they mark boundaries against those above and below. The middle classes reproduce themselves less by passing on property than by converting cultural privilege into educational advantage for their children and then into occupational success. Even the prestige of a detached, ‘Kantian’ aesthetic, appreciating form at a distance from practical need, was a class marker.

Does the theory travel? The most thorough British test, the Cultural Capital and Social Exclusion project, surveyed 1,564 people in 2003–04 and analysed them with Bourdieu's own method. It found three main axes of taste: the first organised by social class and educational qualifications, the second by age and the third by gender. Class still structured culture. But the first axis mainly separated the culturally engaged from the unengaged, and the team found relatively little support for the importance of the Kantian aesthetic or the cultural omnivore as markers of cultural capital.1 Even rock and heavy metal were liked most by men, and, surprisingly, by middle-class, well-educated men.

The omnivore thesis comes from the American sociologist Richard Peterson, who argued from 1992 that high-status taste no longer took a snobbish form but ranged across genres. Others reply that omnivorousness is simply the newest form of cultural capital, since roaming freely across cultural forms requires a distance that only the privileged possess. The balance of evidence suggests Bourdieu identified a real mechanism, the conversion of culture into credentials and credentials into jobs, while the particular map of taste he drew belonged to 1960s France.

title: Foucault: Discipline, Surveillance and Biopower
description: From scaffold to timetable, the Panopticon then and now, biopower and the critics

concepts.title: From the Scaffold to the Timetable
concepts.contentHtml:
Michel Foucault (1926–1984) was a philosopher and historian rather than a sociologist, but few writers have shaped modern sociology more. His work on discourse and knowledge is covered in Structuralism and Poststructuralism; this lesson looks at the account of power that sociologists use. Discipline and Punish (1975) grew out of political work with prisoners. Foucault was a founder of the Groupe d'information sur les prisons and lectured on prisons at the Collège de France two years running.

The book opens with a shock. On 2 March 1757 the would-be regicide Damiens was condemned to make public penance before the main door of the Church of Paris and then to be tortured and torn apart on a scaffold in the Place de Grève. Foucault sets beside it the rules that Léon Faucher drew up eighty years later for a house of young prisoners in Paris: a day measured out by drum-rolls, with rising and dressing in silence, morning prayer, nine hours of work and two hours of instruction. Within a lifetime, punishment moved from a spectacle on the body to a routine aimed at the soul.

Foucault's point is that this was not simply humane progress but the arrival of a new form of power, discipline, which spread through barracks, schools, factories and hospitals. It rests on three techniques:

  • Hierarchical observation: arranging space so that people can be watched.
  • Normalising judgement: measuring everyone against a norm and correcting deviations, rather than simply punishing broken laws.
  • The examination: combining the two and filing the results, which turns each person into a ‘case’.

Discipline produces docile bodies, more useful and easier to control at the same time. Its most provocative conclusion concerns the prison itself, whose real effect, Foucault argued, is to produce criminality and recidivism:1 it categorises its inmates as delinquents, a type of person with a dangerous nature. He even dated the completion of this carceral system to a single day, 22 January 1840, the opening of the reformatory colony at Mettray.

concepts.title: The Panopticon, Then and Now
concepts.contentHtml:
Discipline's emblem is the Panopticon, an ‘inspection house’ that Jeremy Bentham described in 1791 for prisons, asylums and workhouses. A ring of cells surrounds a central tower. Each cell has one window facing out, so the inmate is lit from behind, and one facing the tower, while blinds and partitions hide whoever is inside it. Bentham's principle, as Foucault put it, was that power should be visible and unverifiable: inmates always see the tower but can never tell whether they are being watched at that moment. In his first version Bentham even imagined pipes carrying sound from each cell to the tower.

The effect, Foucault argued, is that the watched begin to watch themselves. Power works automatically, through visibility, and it does not matter who sits in the tower or why. Because the principle can be applied to any institution, a factory, a hospital or a school as easily as a prison, Foucault treated the Panopticon as the architectural model of modern disciplinary power in general.

Two cautions. First, although Foucault is often presented as a theorist of ‘panopticism’, that is not the central claim of his book, which concerns discipline and the prison. Second, anyone applying the image to the present must notice what has changed. Today much watching is done by companies as well as states, it is largely invisible rather than towering, and people know it is happening. In a Pew Research Center survey of 5,101 US adults in May 2023, 71% said they were worried about how the government uses people's data, up from 64% in 2019,1 and 79% felt they had little or no control over what the government does with the data it collects. Bentham's inmates were never sure whether they were being watched; many citizens now assume they always are. Is that panopticism completed, or a different kind of power? Foucault's tools let you ask the question; they do not settle it.

concepts.title: Biopower, Governmentality and the Critics
concepts.contentHtml:
In the first volume of The History of Sexuality (1976) Foucault named a second modern form of power. Sovereign power was founded on violence, the right to kill. Biopower takes life itself as its object, seeking to administer, optimise and multiply it. Its targets are populations, and its techniques coordinate medical care, normalise behaviour, rationalise insurance and rethink urban planning. It is the power of experts and administrators rather than of law, and it needs new knowledge, above all statistics. The same book rejects the ‘repressive hypothesis’, the idea that the Victorians silenced sex, arguing that modern societies multiplied discourses about sexuality instead (the Gender topic applies this).

His lectures of the late 1970s widened the idea into governmentality: government as a set of techniques for managing a population, rather than as the state or the economy. One lecture, published in English as ‘Governmentality’, became the basis of an entire school of sociology and political theory.

Foucault's power is everywhere, which is both his strength and the main charge against him. Critics in the Frankfurt tradition, Habermas above all, accused him of rejecting all normative and rational standards, of lacking a social theory, and of relativism:1 if every norm is an effect of power, on what grounds can discipline be called bad? Nancy Fraser's 1981 essay put the verdict in its title, ‘Foucault on Modern Power: Empirical Insights and Normative Confusions’. Sociologists of punishment objected that one cause cannot explain penal history; David Garland's Punishment and Modern Society set Foucault beside Durkheimian and Marxist accounts and argued for moving beyond the power perspective. Defenders reply that Foucault never claimed power was total: where there is power, he held, there is always resistance too, and his ‘history of the present’ shows that today's arrangements are contingent and so open to change.
